option: Change copays, deductibles and tiers up to the state plan's level
threshold: 30 days with the Public Employee Committee, then a three-person panel decides in 10 days, binding
effect_on_the_gap: Lowers the premium the town buys, so it lowers the rate the whole projection compounds
who_it_lands_on: Employees and retirees, at the point of care — a copay is paid by whoever is ill
note: Copays may be no greater in dollar amount than the GIC's largest non-Medicare plan (§22). Up to 25% of the first year's savings may be directed back to subscribers (§21(f)) — a ceiling on what a panel may order, not a floor the town owes. Lunenburg has never used this route.

option: Move everyone into the state's Group Insurance Commission by agreement
who_decides: Select Board with the Public Employee Committee
threshold: A majority of the weighted votes — the retiree representative holds 10%
effect_on_the_gap: A different premium, and the town stops choosing plans
who_it_lands_on: Everyone insured: the plan menu becomes the state's
note: Notice by 1 December for 1 July. The often-quoted 70% is the threshold for sending a dispute to arbitration, not for agreeing.

option: Move everyone into the GIC without agreement
threshold: Must show savings at least 5% greater than plan design alone could reach (§21(d))
note: Locks the town in for 3 years, then whole-year intervals of at least 2. Benefits are then set exclusively by the Commission and are not bargainable, except the contribution split.

option: Require Medicare-eligible retirees onto a Medicare plan
threshold: Only where the Medicare plan plus Parts A and B is of comparable actuarial value
effect_on_the_gap: Medicare becomes the primary payer, so the town's plan pays only what is left
who_it_lands_on: Retirees, who move to a different plan
note: Lunenburg moved a group in 2020 and states it cut the active renewal 2% and reduced OPEB liability by $5–6M — the town's own figures, with no valuation in the archive.

threshold: Only for someone already covered by a plan financed without any employer participation
effect_on_the_gap: Small: the town saves a premium and pays an incentive
who_it_lands_on: Nobody loses coverage — it is voluntary and reversible
note: Lunenburg's pilot ran from FY24; the Finance Director called the result "minimal." FY27 budgets $14,000 for 10 people.

option: Pay claims from a town trust instead of buying premiums
effect_on_the_gap: Removes the insurer's margin and adds the town's claims risk
note: Any deficit in the claims trust "shall be raised in the next fiscal year's tax rate" — by operation of law. Requires an annual audit accruing claims incurred but not reported.

option: Pay more than half the premium
note: Lunenburg pays 75% for actives. §7A permits more than 50% and has no ceiling — and no route back down.

option: Pay less than half the premium
note: §7 fixes the town's share at 50% and §7A permits "more, but not less, than fifty per cent." There is no downward route in the statute at all.

option: Change the 75/25 split through the plan-design process
note: "The panel shall not impose any change to contribution ratios." The 2011 reform moved plan design out of bargaining and left the split at the table. Between 75% and the 50% floor it is bargained, never decreed.
Acceptance "shall not be revoked or rescinded." And if Town Meeting does not appropriate the cost, §3 has the assessors put it in the tax rate anyway.

option: Drop retirees or require years of service for coverage
note: Galenski v. Town of Erving, 471 Mass. 305 (2015), struck down a ten-year service prerequisite.
